glosses: To cry out suddenly, from some strong emotion.

examples.text:
I am a soldier, and unapt to weep,
Or to exclaim on fortune’s fickleness.
Very grave and good Women exclaimed against Men who begot Children and then disowned them.
This wretched note was the finale of Emma’s breakfast. When once it had been read, there was no doing any thing, but lament and exclaim.
[…] he could remember Sally tearing off a rose, stopping to exclaim at the beauty of the cabbage leaves in the moonlight […]
[…] at the front door below a few guests were leaving, and the bright rectangle widened and narrowed as they slipped out into the night, laughing and exclaiming about the weather.

glosses: To say suddenly and with strong emotion.

examples.text:
Must she be forc’d, t’exclaime th’iniurious wrong?
Offred by him, whom she hath lou’d so long?
Nay, I will tell, and I durst almost sweare,
Edward will blush, when he his fault shall heare.
[…] her aunt, after having stared at me a good while with a look of amazement, exclaimed, “In the name of heaven! Who art thou?”—
Without returning any direct reply, Miss Squeers, all at once, fell into a paroxysm of spiteful tears, and exclaimed that she was a wretched, neglected, miserable castaway.

“Heavens!” exclaimed Nina, “the blue-stocking and the fogy!—and yours are pale blue, Eileen!—you’re about as self-conscious as Drina—slumping there with your hair tumbling à la Mérode! Oh, it's very picturesque, of course, but a straight spine and good grooming is better.[…]”
You never pump your arm when you score, you never exclaim anything, you don’t even smile when you fire a perfect backhand straight down the line.

glosses: Exclamation; outcry, clamor.

examples.text: Oh fortune, thou’rt not worth my least exclame [...].

glosses: To draw in the breath suddenly, as if from a shock.

examples.text: The audience gasped as the magician disappeared.

glosses: To breathe quickly or in a labored manner, as after exertion; to respire with heaving of the breast; to pant.

examples.text: We were all gasping when we reached the summit.

c. 1761-1764, Robert Lloyd, An Epistle to C. Churchill, Author of the Rosicad
She gasps and struggles hard for life.

glosses: To speak in a breathless manner.

examples.text: The old man gasped his last few words.

glosses: To pant with eagerness or excitement; to show vehement desire.

examples.text: I'm gasping for a cup of tea.
Quenching the gasping furrows' thirst with rain.

glosses: A short, sudden intake of breath.

examples.text: The audience gave a gasp of astonishment

glosses: A draw or drag on a cigarette (or gasper).

examples.text: I'm popping out for a gasp.

glosses: The sound of a gasp.

examples.text: Gasp! What will happen next?

glosses: A low, mournful cry of pain, sorrow or pleasure.

examples.text: let out a deep moan
We heard the distant moan of a stag in pain.

glosses: A lament or sorrow.

examples.text: to make one's moan

it shall be my daily grief and moan, that I am so dull, & do so little[…]But if when all is done that we can do, you will leave us nothing but our tears and moans for self-destroyers, the sin is yours, and the suffering shall be yours.

to thee therefore oh Lord do I make my moan, to thee I render my humble petition, and pour out my soul which hath sinned against thee: Oh Lord, I beseech thee for thy infinite mercy in Jesus Christ, to take pity upon mee[…]

glosses: To complain about; to bemoan, to bewail; to mourn.

examples.text: Much did the Craven seeme to mone his case […].

1708, Matthew Prior, the Turtle and the Sparrow
Ye floods, ye woods, ye echoes, moan / My dear Columbo, dead and gone.

glosses: To grieve.
To make a moan or similar sound.

glosses: To say in a moan, or with a moaning voice.

examples.text: ‘Please don't leave me,’ he moaned.

glosses: A deep, prolonged audible inhale and exhale of breath; as when fatigued, frustrated, grieved, or relieved; the act of sighing.

examples.text: To Pollyanna the air was all the more stifling after that cool breath of the out of doors; but she did not complain. She only drew a long quivering sigh.

glosses: a manifestation of grief; a lament.
A person who is bored.

To inhale a larger quantity of air than usual, and immediately expel it; to make a deep single audible respiration, especially as the result or involuntary expression of fatigue, exhaustion, grief, sorrow, frustration, or the like.

examples.text: When she saw it wasn't damaged, she sighed with relief.
He sighed. It was going to be a long night.
He sighed over the lost opportunity.

A waiter brought his aperitif, which was a small scotch and soda, and as he sipped it gratefully he sighed.
 ‘Civilized,’ he said to Mr. Campion. ‘Humanizing.’ […] ‘Cigars and summer days and women in big hats with swansdown face-powder, that's what it reminds me of.’

glosses: To lament; to grieve.

examples.text: He sighed deeply in his spirit.

glosses: To utter sighs over; to lament or mourn over.

examples.text: Ages to come, and men unborn, / Shall bless her name, and sigh her fate.

The lassie had grace given her to refuse, but with a woeful heart, and Heriotside rode off in black discontent, leaving poor Ailie to sigh her love. He came back the next day and the next, but aye he got the same answer.

glosses: To make a sound like sighing.

examples.text: And the coming wind did roar more loud, / And the sails did sigh like sedge.
The winter winds are wearily sighing.

glosses: To exhale (the breath) in sighs.

examples.text: She sighed a sigh that was nearly a groan.
sigh a note and sing a note
Never man sighed truer breath.

glosses: To express by sighs; to utter in or with sighs.

examples.text: "I guess I have no choice," she sighed.
She sighed her frustrations.
They […] sighed forth proverbs.
The gentle swain […] sighs back her grief.

glosses: An expression of fatigue, exhaustion, grief, sorrow, frustration, or the like, often used in casual written contexts.

examples.text: Sigh, I'm so bored at work today.
